claim: α-Synuclein is a presynaptic protein that is implicated in Parkinson's and other neurodegenerative diseases.
source: α-Synuclein is a presynaptic protein that is implicated in Parkinson's and other neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by extensive literature on α-synuclein's role in neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: Native α-synuclein promotes presynaptic SNARE-complex assembly.
source: Physiologically, native α-synuclein promotes presynaptic SNARE-complex assembly, but its molecular mechanism of action remains unknown.
evidence: This statement references established physiological function of α-synuclein, though the mechanism is unknown.

claim: Native α-synuclein promotes clustering of synaptic-vesicle mimics.
source: Here, we found that native α-synuclein promotes clustering of synaptic-vesicle mimics, using a single-vesicle optical microscopy system.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from single-vesicle optical microscopy.

claim: Vesicle-clustering activity was observed for both recombinant and native α-synuclein purified from mouse brain.
source: This vesicle-clustering activity was observed for both recombinant and native α-synuclein purified from mouse brain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing recombinant and brain-purified α-synuclein.

claim: Clustering was dependent on specific interactions of native α-synuclein with both synaptobrevin-2/VAMP2 and anionic lipids.
source: Clustering was dependent on specific interactions of native α-synuclein with both synaptobrevin-2/VAMP2 and anionic lipids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from deletion and mutagenesis studies.

claim: Out of the three familial Parkinson's disease-related point mutants of α-synuclein, only the lipid-binding deficient mutation A30P disrupted clustering.
source: Out of the three familial Parkinson's disease-related point mutants of α-synuclein, only the lipid-binding deficient mutation A30P disrupted clustering, hinting at a possible loss of function phenotype for this mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing the three PD mutants (A30P, E46K, A53T).

claim: The A30P mutation hints at a possible loss of function phenotype.
source: Out of the three familial Parkinson's disease-related point mutants of α-synuclein, only the lipid-binding deficient mutation A30P disrupted clustering, hinting at a possible loss of function phenotype for this mutant.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data on the A30P mutant.

claim: α-Synuclein had little effect on Ca2+-triggered fusion in the reconstituted single-vesicle system.
source: α-Synuclein had little effect on Ca2+-triggered fusion in our reconstituted single-vesicle system, consistent with in vivo data.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the single-vesicle fusion assay.

claim: The lack of effect of α-synuclein on Ca2+-triggered fusion is consistent with in vivo data.
source: α-Synuclein had little effect on Ca2+-triggered fusion in our reconstituted single-vesicle system, consistent with in vivo data.
evidence: This references agreement with previously published in vivo studies.

claim: α-Synuclein may lead to accumulation of synaptic vesicles at the active zone, providing a 'buffer' of synaptic vesicles, without affecting neurotransmitter release itself.
source: α-Synuclein may therefore lead to accumulation of synaptic vesicles at the active zone, providing a 'buffer' of synaptic vesicles, without affecting neurotransmitter release itself.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: α-Synuclein is an abundant presynaptic protein that is expressed throughout the central nervous system (CNS) and associated with synaptic vesicles.
source: α-Synuclein (α-Syn) is an abundant presynaptic protein that is expressed throughout the central nervous system (CNS) and associated with synaptic vesicles (Maroteaux et al., 1988; Jensen et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Missense mutations (A30P, E46K, A53T) of α-Syn are linked to early onset Parkinson's disease (PD).
source: Pathologically, missense mutations (A30P, E46K, A53T) of α-Syn (Polymeropoulos et al., 1997; Kruger et al., 1998; Zarranz et al., 2004) and duplications and triplications of the gene that encodes α-Syn (Singleton et al., 2003; Chartier-Harlin et al., 2004) are linked to early onset Parkinson's disease (PD).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Duplications and triplications of the gene that encodes α-Syn are linked to early onset Parkinson's disease (PD).
source: Pathologically, missense mutations (A30P, E46K, A53T) of α-Syn (Polymeropoulos et al., 1997; Kruger et al., 1998; Zarranz et al., 2004) and duplications and triplications of the gene that encodes α-Syn (Singleton et al., 2003; Chartier-Harlin et al., 2004) are linked to early onset Parkinson's disease (PD).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lewy bodies observed in Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and other neurodegenerative diseases contain high concentrations of α-Syn aggregates.
source: Moreover, Lewy bodies observed in Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and other neurodegenerative diseases contain high concentrations of α-Syn aggregates (Spillantini et al., 1997; Hardy and Gwinn-Hardy, 1998; Spillantini et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In aqueous solution, α-Syn is a largely unfolded protein and has a propensity to aggregate in a nucleation-dependent manner, forming β-sheet rich amyloid-like fibrils.
source: In aqueous solution, α-Syn is a largely unfolded protein and has a propensity to aggregate in a nucleation-dependent manner, forming β-sheet rich amyloid-like fibrils (Serpell et al., 2000; Zhao et al., 2011; Burré et al., In press).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fibrils, protofibrils and/or large oligomers are believed to be cytotoxic.
source: Fibrils, protofibrils and/or large oligomers are believed to be cytotoxic (Conway et al., 2000; Goldberg and Lansbury, 2000; Bucciantini et al., 2002), and may be responsible, at least in part, for the neurodegeneration observed in diseases featuring Lewy bodies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cytotoxic α-synuclein species may be responsible, at least in part, for the neurodegeneration observed in diseases featuring Lewy bodies.
source: Fibrils, protofibrils and/or large oligomers are believed to be cytotoxic (Conway et al., 2000; Goldberg and Lansbury, 2000; Bucciantini et al., 2002), and may be responsible, at least in part, for the neurodegeneration observed in diseases featuring Lewy bodies.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on cited literature.

claim: α-Syn increases the rate of SNARE-complex formation at the synapse via binding to the SNARE protein synaptobrevin-2 and to phospholipids.
source: Physiologically, α-Syn increases the rate of SNARE-complex formation at the synapse via binding to the SNARE protein synaptobrevin-2 (also called VAMP2, vesicle associated membrane protein 2) and to phospholipids (Burré et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In adult canaries and zebra finches, α-Syn expression correlates with plasticity in the developing song control system.
source: In adult canaries and zebra finches, α-Syn expression correlates with plasticity in the developing song control system (Clayton and George, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Deletion of α-Syn in mice has been reported to show either no or very small and opposing effects on neurotransmitter release.
source: However, deletion of α-Syn in mice has been reported to show either no or very small and opposing effects on neurotransmitter release (Abeliovich et al., 2000; Cabin et al., 2002; Chandra et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2004; Yavich et al., 2004; Unger et al., 2006; Senior et al., 2008; Burré et al., 2010; Garcia-Reitbock et al., 2010; Scott et al., 2010; Anwar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Overexpression of α-Syn either in transgenic mice or using stereotactic injections of adeno-associated virus have resulted in conflicting effects on neurotransmitter release.
source: Similarly, overexpression of α-Syn either in transgenic mice or using stereotactic injections of adeno-associated virus have resulted in conflicting effects on neurotransmitter release, although chronic overexpression nearly always leads to neurodegeneration (Liu et al., 2004; Larsen et al., 2006; Burré et al., 2010; Nemani et al., 2010; Gaugler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chronic overexpression of α-Syn nearly always leads to neurodegeneration.
source: Similarly, overexpression of α-Syn either in transgenic mice or using stereotactic injections of adeno-associated virus have resulted in conflicting effects on neurotransmitter release, although chronic overexpression nearly always leads to neurodegeneration (Liu et al., 2004; Larsen et al., 2006; Burré et al., 2010; Nemani et al., 2010; Gaugler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: α-Syn is a 14-kDa protein composed of an amphipathic, positively charged 100 residue N-terminal domain with a lysine-rich N-terminus that binds reversibly to anionic membranes.
source: Structurally, α-Syn is a 14-kDa protein composed of an amphipathic, positively charged 100 residue N-terminal domain with a lysine-rich N-terminus that binds reversibly to anionic membranes (Rhoades et al., 2006), and a 40-residue highly acidic C-terminal domain that interacts with the N-terminal sequence of synaptobrevin-2 (Burré et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: α-Syn has a 40-residue highly acidic C-terminal domain that interacts with the N-terminal sequence of synaptobrevin-2.
source: Structurally, α-Syn is a 14-kDa protein composed of an amphipathic, positively charged 100 residue N-terminal domain with a lysine-rich N-terminus that binds reversibly to anionic membranes (Rhoades et al., 2006), and a 40-residue highly acidic C-terminal domain that interacts with the N-terminal sequence of synaptobrevin-2 (Burré et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Recombinant, erythrocyte, and brain α-Syn is predominantly monomeric in solution with a smaller fraction of multimeric species, and is largely unstructured with a small (approximately 21–24%) helical contribution.
source: Recombinant, erythrocyte, and brain α-Syn is predominantly monomeric in solution with a smaller fraction of multimeric species, and is largely unstructured with a small (approximately 21–24%) helical contribution (Fauvet et al., 2012; Burré et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At high concentrations (∼500 μM) and in the presence of β-octylglucoside, nuclear magnetic resonance spectra showed weak intramolecular NOEs in regions of α-helical propensity but no tertiary interactions, reminiscent of a molten globule.
source: At high concentrations (∼500 μM) and in the presence of β-octylglucoside, nuclear magnetic resonance spectra showed weak intramolecular NOEs in regions of α-helical propensity but no tertiary interactions, reminiscent of a molten globule (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The interaction with anionic lipids induces α-helicity in α-Syn, as revealed by CD spectroscopy.
source: The interaction with anionic lipids induces α-helicity in α-Syn, as revealed by CD spectroscopy (Davidson et al., 1998; Jo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Solution NMR studies, EPR analyses, calorimetry, and single molecule fluorescence resonance transfer experiments in the presence of SDS micelles and small unilamellar vesicles revealed that the N-terminal 100 residues form a broken amphiphatic α-helix upon binding to anionic lipids.
source: Moreover, solution NMR studies, EPR analyses, calorimetry, and single molecule fluorescence resonance transfer experiments in the presence of SDS micelles and small unilamellar vesicles revealed that the N-terminal 100 residues form a broken amphiphatic α-helix upon binding to anionic lipids (Bussell and Eliezer, 2003; Chandra et al., 2003; Ulmer et al., 2005; Jao et al., 2008; Ferreon et al., 2009; Lokappa and Ulmer, 2011; Maltsev et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Binding of α-Syn to the membrane is transient.
source: Binding of α-Syn to the membrane is transient, and the C-terminal 40 residues of α-Syn are unstructured and not bound to the membrane (Bodner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The C-terminal 40 residues of α-Syn are unstructured and not bound to the membrane.
source: Binding of α-Syn to the membrane is transient, and the C-terminal 40 residues of α-Syn are unstructured and not bound to the membrane (Bodner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: N-terminal acetylation of α-Syn does not induce significant structure in recombinant α-Syn in solution (i.e., absence of detergents or lipids), but further enhances its binding to anionic membranes and induced α-helicity.
source: N-terminal acetylation of α-Syn does not induce significant structure in recombinant α-Syn in solution (i.e., absence of detergents or lipids), but further enhances its binding to anionic membranes and induced α-helicity (Maltsev et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Although initially largely monomeric, purified brain α-Syn associates into partially folded multimers and aggregates in a time-dependent manner.
source: Although initially largely monomeric, purified brain α-Syn associates into partially folded multimers and aggregates in a time-dependent manner (Burré et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Different monomeric and oligomeric states of α-Syn likely exist in an equilibrium in vivo, which is modulated by a variety of factors and interactions, such as membrane binding.
source: It is likely that these different monomeric and oligomeric states exist in an equilibrium in vivo, which is modulated by a variety of factors and interactions, such as membrane binding.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the cited data.

claim: The labile mixture of conformations provides a potential explanation for why α-Syn is so susceptible to pathological aggregation and fibril formation as observed in multiple neurodegenerative disorders.
source: This labile mixture of conformations provides a potential explanation for why α-Syn is so susceptible to pathological aggregation and fibril formation as observed in multiple neurodegenerative disorders (Devine et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Native α-Syn does not significantly affect the efficiency and kinetics of Ca2+-triggered synaptic protein-mediated fusion itself.
source: We found that native α-Syn does not significantly affect the efficiency and kinetics of Ca2+-triggered synaptic protein-mediated fusion itself.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the single-vesicle fusion assay.

claim: α-Syn induces clustering of vesicles with reconstituted synaptobrevin-2 or with both reconstituted synaptobrevin-2 and synaptotagmin-1.
source: Rather, α-Syn induces clustering of vesicles with reconstituted synaptobrevin-2 or with both reconstituted synaptobrevin-2 and synaptotagmin-1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the clustering assay.

claim: The clustering effect is dependent on specific binding to both anionic lipid membranes and synaptobrevin-2 as revealed by deletion and mutagenesis studies.
source: The clustering effect is dependent on specific binding to both anionic lipid membranes and synaptobrevin-2 as revealed by deletion and mutagenesis studies, including the Parkinson's disease mutant A30P that disrupts lipid binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from deletion and mutagenesis studies.

claim: The Parkinson's disease mutant A30P disrupts lipid binding.
source: The clustering effect is dependent on specific binding to both anionic lipid membranes and synaptobrevin-2 as revealed by deletion and mutagenesis studies, including the Parkinson's disease mutant A30P that disrupts lipid binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on the A30P mutant.

claim: Clustering is induced by both recombinant and brain-purified native α-Syn, both of which are initially in a largely monomeric state in the absence of membranes.
source: Furthermore, clustering is induced by both recombinant and brain-purified native α-Syn, both of which are initially in a largely monomeric state in the absence of membranes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing recombinant and brain-purified α-Syn.

claim: The clustering or lack thereof may account for the increase in SNARE-complex levels observed upon overexpression of native α-Syn.
source: This clustering or lack thereof may account for the increase in SNARE-complex levels observed upon overexpression of native α-Syn (Burré et al., 2010), and, conversely, the decrease in SNARE-complex assembly in αβγ-Syn triple knockout mice (Burré et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by citation.

claim: The clustering or lack thereof may account for the decrease in SNARE-complex assembly in αβγ-Syn triple knockout mice.
source: This clustering or lack thereof may account for the increase in SNARE-complex levels observed upon overexpression of native α-Syn (Burré et al., 2010), and, conversely, the decrease in SNARE-complex assembly in αβγ-Syn triple knockout mice (Burré et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by citation.

claim: In the absence of α-Syn, 166 fusion events were observed out of ∼2000 docked v-vesicles within the observation period of 50 s.
source: In the absence of α-Syn, we observed 166 fusion events out of ∼2000 docked v-vesicles (identified as fluorescent spots that were present prior to Ca2+ injection), whereas in the presence of α-Syn, we observed 84 fusion events out of ∼1300 docked v-vesicles within the observation period of 50 s.
evidence: This is experimental data from the Ca2+-triggered fusion assay, shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the presence of α-Syn, 84 fusion events were observed out of ∼1300 docked v-vesicles within the observation period of 50 s.
source: In the absence of α-Syn, we observed 166 fusion events out of ∼2000 docked v-vesicles (identified as fluorescent spots that were present prior to Ca2+ injection), whereas in the presence of α-Syn, we observed 84 fusion events out of ∼1300 docked v-vesicles within the observation period of 50 s.
evidence: This is experimental data from the Ca2+-triggered fusion assay, shown in Figure 1.

claim: Native α-Syn reduced the number of fluorescent spots that appeared when v-vesicles bound to immobilized t-vesicles during the incubation stage at zero Ca2+.
source: Although native α-Syn showed no effect on Ca2+-triggered fusion activity, we noticed that α-Syn reduced the number of fluorescent spots that appeared when v-vesicles bound to immobilized t-vesicles during the incubation stage at zero Ca2+ (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data from the v-/t-vesicle association assay, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The addition of native α-Syn produced the emergence of brighter spots between 1.5 and 6 a.u. in the fluorescence emission histogram.
source: However, the addition of native α-Syn produced the emergence of brighter spots between 1.5 and 6 a.u. in the fluorescence emission histogram (insert, Figure 2B), along with occasional very large fluorescent spots (black arrow, lower right image in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data from the fluorescence intensity distribution, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The major peak (<1.5 a.u.) at low fluorescence intensity corresponds to single donor v-vesicles docked to the imaging surface.
source: The major peak (<1.5 a.u.) at low fluorescence intensity corresponds to single donor v-vesicles docked to the imaging surface, while the high intensity tail (>2 a.u.) corresponds to small clusters of v-vesicles docked to the surface.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fluorescence intensity distribution data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The high intensity tail (>2 a.u.) corresponds to small clusters of v-vesicles docked to the surface.
source: The major peak (<1.5 a.u.) at low fluorescence intensity corresponds to single donor v-vesicles docked to the imaging surface, while the high intensity tail (>2 a.u.) corresponds to small clusters of v-vesicles docked to the surface.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fluorescence intensity distribution data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the presence of α-Syn, a reduction of the single vesicle population and a concomitant increase of a population of vesicle clusters was observed.
source: In the presence of α-Syn, we thus observed a reduction of the single vesicle population and a concomitant increase of a population of vesicle clusters.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fluorescence intensity distribution data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The observed decrease in the total number of fluorescent spots in the presence of native α-Syn can be explained by a reduction of the number of free-floating particles by clustering of individual v-vesicles in the finite volume of the sample chamber.
source: Thus, the observed decrease in the total number of fluorescent spots (referred to as 'v-/t-vesicle associations') in the presence of native α-Syn (Figure 2A) can be explained by a reduction of the number of free-floating particles by clustering of individual v-vesicles in the finite volume of the sample chamber (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 2A and illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: Native α-Syn increases the clustering of v-vesicles in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Using this clustering assay, we confirmed that native α-Syn increases the clustering of v-vesicles in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is experimental data from the v-/v-vesicle clustering assay, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The buffer exchange removed unbound α-Syn.
source: Subsequent to the incubation stage, a buffer exchange with α-Syn-free buffer was performed for 6 s which removed unbound α-Syn.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: The buffer exchange likely removed some of the v-vesicle-bound α-Syn molecules since kinetic studies by NMR spectroscopy revealed that α-Syn binding to membranes is transient with exchanges occurring in the range of 1–10 s-1.
source: Moreover, it is likely that the buffer exchange also removed some of the v-vesicle-bound α-Syn molecules since kinetic studies by NMR spectroscopy revealed that α-Syn binding to membranes is transient with exchanges occurring in the range of 1–10 s-1 (Bodner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited NMR kinetic data.

claim: The effective α-Syn concentration during the final clustering step is lower than 2–20 μM, as only bound α-Syn is present at this stage.
source: Thus, the effective α-Syn concentration during the final clustering step (Figure 3B, right panel) is lower than 2–20 μM, as only bound α-Syn is present at this stage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental protocol and the transient binding of α-Syn.

claim: V-vesicle clustering has not reached saturation at 2 μM α-Syn incubation concentration.
source: Indeed, as Figure 4A shows, v-vesicle clustering has not reached saturation at 2 μM α-Syn incubation concentration, so v-vesicles were not fully covered with α-Syn molecules at that particular α-Syn incubation concentration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the concentration-dependent data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: V-vesicles were not fully covered with α-Syn molecules at 2 μM α-Syn incubation concentration.
source: Indeed, as Figure 4A shows, v-vesicle clustering has not reached saturation at 2 μM α-Syn incubation concentration, so v-vesicles were not fully covered with α-Syn molecules at that particular α-Syn incubation concentration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the concentration-dependent data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A cryo-electron microscopy experiment revealed large v-vesicle clusters in the presence of native α-Syn.
source: As another independent confirmation of v-vesicle clustering, a cryo-electron microscopy experiment revealed large v-vesicle clusters in the presence of native α-Syn (Figure 5).
evidence: This is experimental data from cryo-EM, shown in Figure 5.

claim: The vesicle concentration used for the cryo-EM experiment was 100-fold higher than that used for the single-vesicle clustering experiments.
source: Note, that the vesicle concentration used for the cryo-EM experiment was 100-fold higher and the effective α-Syn concentration was also higher than that used for the single-vesicle clustering experiments, explaining the formation of the fairly large clusters in the cryo-EM experiment at that concentration.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions for the cryo-EM experiment.

claim: V-vesicles clustering does not occur in the absence of α-Syn.
source: V-vesicles clustering does not occur in the absence of α-Syn (Kyoung et al., 2011) and is therefore specific to native α-Syn.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: V-vesicle clustering is specific to native α-Syn.
source: V-vesicles clustering does not occur in the absence of α-Syn (Kyoung et al., 2011) and is therefore specific to native α-Syn.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: V-vesicle clustering is entirely dependent on the presence of synaptobrevin-2.
source: It is also entirely dependent on the presence of synaptobrevin-2, as lack of synaptobrevin-2 (Figure 4A), or truncation of C-terminal residues of α-Syn that bind to synaptobrevin-2 (Burré et al., 2010) but do not participate in lipid binding of α-Syn (Burré et al., 2010, 2012) significantly reduced clustering of v-vesicles (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A, 4B, and 4C, and citations.

claim: Truncation of C-terminal residues of α-Syn that bind to synaptobrevin-2 significantly reduced clustering of v-vesicles.
source: It is also entirely dependent on the presence of synaptobrevin-2, as lack of synaptobrevin-2 (Figure 4A), or truncation of C-terminal residues of α-Syn that bind to synaptobrevin-2 (Burré et al., 2010) but do not participate in lipid binding of α-Syn (Burré et al., 2010, 2012) significantly reduced clustering of v-vesicles (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 4C, and citations.

claim: Clustering of v-vesicles depended on the presence of negatively charged (anionic) lipids.
source: Furthermore, clustering of v-vesicles depended on the presence of negatively charged (anionic) lipids (Figure 4A, right most condition), which is known to induce α-helix formation in native α-Syn and lipid binding of α-Syn.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Negatively charged lipids are known to induce α-helix formation in native α-Syn and lipid binding of α-Syn.
source: Furthermore, clustering of v-vesicles depended on the presence of negatively charged (anionic) lipids (Figure 4A, right most condition), which is known to induce α-helix formation in native α-Syn and lipid binding of α-Syn.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: α-helicity was observed in the CD spectrum of native α-Syn in the presence of protein-free vesicles with the same lipid composition used for the fusion and v-vesicle clustering experiments.
source: As a control, and in agreement with previous studies (Davidson et al., 1998; Jo et al., 2000; Eliezer et al., 2001), we observed α-helicity in the CD spectrum of native α-Syn in the presence of protein-free vesicles with the same lipid composition used for our fusion and v-vesicle clustering experiments (Figure 6).
evidence: This is experimental data from CD spectroscopy, shown in Figure 6, and supported by citations.

claim: Native α-Syn has to bind to both synaptobrevin-2 and anionic lipids in order to cluster v-vesicles.
source: Taken together, our clustering experiments suggest that native α-Syn has to bind to both, synaptobrevin-2 and anionic lipids, in order to cluster v-vesicles, confirming the protein- and anionic-lipid specificity of this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from the clustering experiments.

claim: V-vesicle clustering induced by native α-Syn was similar with and without synaptotagmin-1 within experimental error.
source: We found that v-vesicle clustering induced by native α-Syn was similar with and without synaptotagmin-1 within experimental error.
evidence: This is experimental data from the clustering assay with different vesicle compositions, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: V-vesicles with only reconstituted synaptotagmin-1 did not cluster.
source: Furthermore, v-vesicles with only reconstituted synaptotagmin-1 did not cluster, consistent with the requirement of synaptobrevin-2 for native α-Syn-induced v-vesicle clustering (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is experimental data from the clustering assay, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All three PD-related mutants (A30P, E46K, A53T) retain the ability to bind synaptobrevin-2.
source: While all these mutants retain the ability to bind synaptobrevin-2, only A30P shows reduced membrane binding (Burré et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Only A30P shows reduced membrane binding among the three PD-related mutants.
source: While all these mutants retain the ability to bind synaptobrevin-2, only A30P shows reduced membrane binding (Burré et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Out of the mutants tested, only A30P showed ∼ 50% decrease in membrane binding compared to native wildtype α-Syn.
source: Out of the mutants tested, only A30P showed ∼ 50% decrease in membrane binding and v-vesicle clustering compared to native wildtype α-Syn.
evidence: This is experimental data from the lipid flotation assay, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Out of the mutants tested, only A30P showed ∼ 50% decrease in v-vesicle clustering compared to native wildtype α-Syn.
source: Out of the mutants tested, only A30P showed ∼ 50% decrease in membrane binding and v-vesicle clustering compared to native wildtype α-Syn.
evidence: This is experimental data from the clustering assay, shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The effect of the three mutations in v-vesicle clustering correlated well with their effect on native α-Syn binding to PS-containing vesicles.
source: Thus, the effect of the three mutations in v-vesicle clustering correlated well with their effect on native α-Syn binding to PS-containing vesicles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Membrane-binding by native α-Syn is essential for its clustering activity.
source: This suggests that membrane-binding by native α-Syn is essential for its clustering activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation between membrane binding and clustering activity.

claim: Only the A30P mutant increased the number of v-/t-vesicle associations.
source: Only the A30P mutant increased the number of v-/t-vesicle associations.
evidence: This is experimental data from the v-/t-vesicle association assay, shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The reduction of the number of v-/t-vesicle associations by native wildtype α-Syn is a consequence of the finite volume used during the incubation stage and the reduction of the number of free particles in the sample chamber by v-vesicle clustering.
source: As mentioned above, the reduction of the number of v-/t-vesicle associations by native wildtype α-Syn is a consequence of the finite volume used during the incubation stage and the reduction of the number of free particles in the sample chamber by v-vesicle clustering.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: The numbers of v-vesicle clusters and v-/t-vesicle associations are anti-correlated.
source: Thus, the numbers of v-vesicle clusters (Figure 7C) and v-/t-vesicle associations (Figure 7D) are anti-correlated.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: Native α-Syn was purified from mouse brain without detergents or denaturants using multiple chromatography steps to a purity of >90%.
source: In order to test whether native brain-purified α-Syn has the same activity as native recombinant α-Syn in clustering v-vesicles, we purified native α-Syn from mouse brain without detergents or denaturants using multiple chromatography steps to a purity of >90% (Burré et al., In press).
evidence: This is a description of the purification method, supported by citation.

claim: The induction of v-vesicle clustering by native brain purified α-Syn was similar to that of native recombinant α-Syn.
source: We found that the induction of v-vesicle clustering by native brain purified α-Syn was similar to that of native recombinant α-Syn (compare Figures 4A and 8), confirming that the observed clustering activity is not sensitive to the origin of α-Syn.
evidence: This is experimental data comparing recombinant and brain-purified α-Syn, shown in Figures 4A and 8.

claim: The observed clustering activity is not sensitive to the origin of α-Syn.

claim: Transgenic mice with overexpressed human α-Syn invariably exhibit signs of neurodegeneration.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Impairment in synaptic vesicle exocytosis and a reduction in neurotransmitter release were observed only in some studies of transgenic mice with overexpressed human α-Syn.
source: Transgenic mice with overexpressed human α-Syn invariably exhibit signs of neurodegeneration, but impairment in synaptic vesicle exocytosis and a reduction in neurotransmitter release were observed only in some studies (Nemani et al., 2010; Scott et al., 2010) but not in another study (Burré et al., 2010).

claim: While native α-Syn clusters v-vesicles and reduces the number of free particles in the v-/t-vesicle assay without interfering with SNARE interactions, large α-Syn oligomers interfere with SNARE complex formation and reduce docking.
source: We note that although both our v-/t-vesicle assay and the single-vesicle lipid mixing assay by (Choi et al., 2013) revealed a reduction of the number of fluorescent ('docked') spots in v-/t-vesicle experiments, the underlying mechanism is different: while native α-Syn clusters v-vesicles and reduces the number of free particles in our v-/t-vesicle assay without interfering with SNARE interactions, large α-Syn oligomers interfere with SNARE complex formation and reduce docking in the lipid mixing assay of (Choi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of the mechanisms between the current study and a cited study.
